oaken.e: Inherited from Middle English oken (also eken), from Old English ācen, ǣċen (“of oak”), from Proto-Germanic *aikīnaz, equivalent to oak + -en (adjectival suffix).
oaken.x: His knuckles are tattooed, his hands the oaken tools of the boxer he still is, now as a coach.

oakwood.e: From Old English āc wudu; equivalent to oak + wood.
oakwood.x: The Marlfox ignored the jibe, listening to the steady ring of axeblades against oakwood.

oasis.e: From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25 Compare Sahidic Coptic ⲟⲩⲁϩⲉ…
oasis.x: The park was an oasis in the middle of the busy city.

oatmeal.e: From Middle English otemele, from ote (“oat”) + mele (“meal, coarse-ground grains”). Equivalent to oat + meal.

obdurate.e: First attested in the 1450s, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English obdurat(e), borrowed from Latin obdūrātus (“hardened”), perfect passive participle of obdūrō…
obdurate.x: But custom maketh blind and obdurate The loftiest hearts.

obedience.e: From Middle English obedience, from Anglo-Norman obedience, from Old French obedience (modern French obédience), from Latin oboedientia.
obedience.x: Obedience is essential in any army.

obelisk.e: From Middle French obelisque, from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”). Compare obelus.

obesity.e: From French obésité, from Latin obēsitās, from obēsus (“fat”). By surface analysis, obese + -ity.

obfuscate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1487, in Middle English, the verb in 1536.
obfuscate.x: The squid's ink obfuscated its presence.

obituary.e: PIE word *h₁epi Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obituārius (“obituary”) + English -ary (suffix denoting something relating to another thing or used in a place).

objective.e: From Middle English obgectyf, from Middle French objectif and its etymon Medieval Latin obiectīvus. By surface analysis, object + -ive.
objective.x: The value of pedagogical material informed by objective methodological procedures developed in corpus linguistics is widely recognized.

objectivity.x: The scientist’s objectivity was questioned after the funding controversy.

oblation.e: From Middle English oblacioun, from Old French oblacion, from Latin oblātiō (“offering”), from offerō (“to offer, present”). By surface analysis, oblate + -ion.
oblation.x: And if thy oblation be a meate offering baken in the frying pan,it ſhalbe made of fine flowꝛe with oyle.

obligation.e: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio, obligationem, from obligatum (past participle of obligare), from ob- (“to”) + ligare…
obligation.x: I feel I'm under obligation to attend my sister's wedding, even though we have a very frosty relationship.

oblige.e: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.
oblige.x: Your carelessness obliges firmness on my part.

obliged.x: All employees are obliged to complete a tax return every year.

oblique.e: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).
oblique.x: Italic fonts are sometimes described as oblique in typographic terminology.

obliterate.e: PIE word *h₁epi (start of 17th century) From earlier obliterat, learned borrowing from Latin obliterātus, oblitterātus (“having been blotted out, effaced, erased.
obliterate.x: Soham's station had been completely obliterated (the replacement was to close in 1965 and is only now being reopened).

oblivion.e: Inherited from Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).
oblivion.x: He regularly drank himself into oblivion.

oblivious.e: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”)…
oblivious.x: Your grandmother is completely oblivious to her surroundings.

oblong.e: From Middle English oblong, oblonge, borrowed from Latin oblongus.

obnoxious.x: Throwing stones at the bus is another example of your obnoxious behaviour.

obscene.e: From Middle French obscene (modern French obscène (“indecent, obscene”)), and from its etymon Latin obscēnus, obscaenus (“inauspicious; ominous; disgusting, filthy.
obscene.x: What is obscene today may not be so tomorrow or what is obscene at one place may not be obscene at another place.

obscenity.x: The coalition of religious conservatives was campaigning against, in their view, rampant obscenity in the entertainment industry.

obscurantism.e: From Latin obscūrans, from obscūrō (“to cover, darken, obscure”) + -ism.

obscure.e: From Middle English obscure, from Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from ob- + *scūrus, from Proto-Italic *skoiros, from…
obscure.x: His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness.

obscurity.e: From Middle English obscurite, obscuryte, from Middle French obscurité and its etymon Latin obscūritās. By surface analysis, obscure + -ity.
obscurity.x: She was plucked from obscurity to star in a Broadway musical.

observant.x: The observant police officer noticed that my tax disk was out-of-date.

observation.e: From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Also a borrowing from French observation and a learned borrowing from Latin observātiō(n-).
observation.x: To observations which ourselves we make / We grow more partial for the observer's sake.

observatory.e: Borrowed from French observatoire, equivalent to observe + -atory.
observatory.x: The corporation of Harvard University have passed a vote closing the observatory in Cambridge to the public on Saturday evenings.

observer.x: Most impartial observers agreed that Sampras had not served well.

obsess.e: From Latin obsessus, perfect passive participle of obsideō (“sit on or in, remain, besiege”), from ob- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”); see sit, session, etc..
obsess.x: Some people are obsessed with sports.

obsession.e: From Latin obsessio (“a besieging”), from obsidere (“to besiege”); see obsess. Equivalent to obsess + -ion.
obsession.x: My obsession with rugby resulted in me spending years following the sport.

obsessive.x: The idea is too tempting, it's obsessive.

obsidian.e: From Latin obsidianus; named after Obsidius, who was, according to Pliny, the Roman who discovered the stone in Aethiopia.

obsolete.x: Speedy, worldwide, accessible delivery of news through the Web has made newspapers obsolete.

obstacle.e: From Middle English obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.
obstacle.x: A big obstacle to understanding the manual was that it had been poorly translated from the Japanese.

obstinacy.x: He finished only through a mixture of determined obstinacy and ingenuity.

obstinate.e: Inherited from Middle English obstinat(e) (“obstinate, stubborn”), from Latin obstinātus, perfect passive participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”)…
obstinate.x: He had the same pile of curly hair, but he was clean-shaven with a heavy, obstinate jowl.

obstruct.e: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).

obstruction.e: From Latin obstructio (“hindrance”), from obstruo (“build against, block, stop”).
obstruction.x: The referee stopped play because of an obstruction by the defender.

obtain.e: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- +…
obtain.x: Applicants must obtain a permit before construction.

obtuse.e: From Middle English obtuse, from Latin obtūsus (“blunt, dull; obtuse”), past participle of obtundere, from obtundō (“to batter, beat, strike.
obtuse.x: For we see a Feather or a Rush drawn along the Lip or Cheek, doth tickle; whereas a thing more obtuse, or a touch more hard, doth not.

occasional.e: From Middle English occasyonal, from Medieval Latin occāsiōnālis and Old French ocasionel. By surface analysis, occasion + -al.
occasional.x: Elgar's music was not created to be occasional music for high-school graduations.

occasionally.e: From Middle English occasionally, occasionaly, occasyoneely, occasyonly, equivalent to occasional + -ly.
occasionally.x: Some perhaps worship only on alternate Sundays; others still more occasionally.

occultism.e: Borrowed from French occultisme, analyzable as occult + -ism.

occupant.e: Borrowed from Middle French occupant (present participle of occuper) or Latin occupāns, occupantis (present participle of occupō). By surface analysis, occupy + -ant.
occupant.x: I looked over to the Radley Place, expecting to see its phantom occupant sunning himself in the swing. The swing was empty.

occupation.e: From Middle English occupacioun, borrowed from Middle French occupacion, occupation, from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnis, from occupō (“occupy, seize”), ultimately from…
occupation.x: The early years of Norman occupation saw a frenzy of castle building.

occupied.x: My father travelled to occupied Japan in December 1945.

occupy.e: From Middle English occupien, occupyen, borrowed from Old French occuper, from Latin occupāre (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from ob (“to…
occupy.x: I occupy myself with gardening for a few hours every day.

occur.e: Originally "meet (in argument)", borrowed from Middle French occurrer, from Latin occurrō (“run to meet, run against, befall, present itself”) from prefix ob- (“against”)…
occur.x: The liftoff will occur in exactly twelve seconds.

occurrence.e: From Middle French occurrence, from Medieval Latin occurrentia. Morphologically occur + -ence.

ocelot.e: From French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Classical Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).

ochre.e: From Old French ocre and its source Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).

octagon.e: From Latin octagōnon, octōgōnon (“octagon”), and from its etymon Ancient Greek ὀκτάγωνον (oktágōnon, “octagon”), probably from Koine Greek ὀκτάγωνος (oktágōnos, “having…

octagonal.x: The sundials range in shape from octagonal to the usual round. Prices range from $75 to $375.

octahedron.e: From Ancient Greek ὀκτάεδρον (oktáedron). By surface analysis, octa- + -hedron.

octave.e: From Latin octavus (“eighth”). Doublet of octavo, ochava, and oitava.
octave.x: The melody jumps up an octave at the beginning, then later drops back down an octave.

octopus.x: Even octopuses without stylets almost certainly retain the molecular machinery necessary to build them.

odalisque.e: Borrowed from French odalisque, from Ottoman Turkish اوطهلق (odalık, “chambermaid”), from اوده (oda, “room”).

oddball.e: Compound of odd + ball. First used in late 1930s, describing an extra ball played as a bonus in pin-ball type games.
oddball.x: "She's different, mister. A real oddball, if you know what I mean. But your little girl would love her. All kids love the Doll Lady."

odeon.e: From Ancient Greek ᾠδεῖον (ōideîon), from ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or…

odious.e: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).
odious.x: Scrubbing the toilets in the bar at the end of a Saturday night is an odious task.

odometer.e: From French odomètre, from Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road, path, way”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to odo- + -meter.

odorless.x: They were taken unawares and overcome when the room filled with a lethal, odorless gas.

odorous.e: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.
odorous.x: The table was piled with odorous lilies.

odyssey.e: From Odyssey, from Ancient Greek Ὀδυσσεία (Odusseía, “the story of Odysseus”).
odyssey.x: Many have been sharing cartoons praying for a successful conclusion to the Wild Boar team's odyssey, hoping that it will end in their safe rescue.

oesophagus.e: From Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos), from οἴσω (oísō), future form of φέρω (phérō, “to carry”) + ἔφαγον (éphagon, “to eat”).
oesophagus.x: Graham, who lived in Somersham, Cambridgeshire, donated his oesophagus to the MRC cancer unit at Cambridge University, for research.

oeuvre.e: From French œuvre, from Old French uevre, from Latin opera (plural of Latin opus), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”). Doublet of opera, opus, and ure.
oeuvre.x: Let’s “fictionalize” Foucault’s life by turning it into a biographical account of Foucault and his oeuvre or work.

offal.e: From Middle English offal, offall, offalle (“offal, refuse, scrap waste”), equivalent to off- + fall.
offal.x: All the insides clean and compact, coming out all together. Nick tossed the offal ashore for the minks to find.

offend.e: From Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō (“strike, blunder, commit an offense”), from ob- (“against”) + *fendō (“strike”).
offend.x: Don't worry. I don't offend easily.

offender.e: From Middle English offendour, offender, offendir, equivalent to offend + -er.

offensive.e: From Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if by analogy with défensif. Offendre is from Latin offendere (“to offend”); see offend.

offset.e: From off- + set, used to construct the noun form of the verb to set off.
offset.x: Today's victory was an offset to yesterday's defeat.

offshore.x: American companies use offshore services for one reason, said Herbert F. Schantz, a consultant in Sterling, Va.: cheap labor.

offside.e: From off- + side. Compare German Abseite (“remote area, backside”), German abseits (“out of the way, apart, aside”, adverb), Dutch afzijdig (“neutral, impartial”).

offspring.e: From Middle English ofspring, from Old English ofspring (“offspring, descendants, posterity”), equivalent to off- + spring. Compare Icelandic afspringur (“offspring”).
offspring.x: We are the offspring of Italian immigrants.

oftentimes.e: Inherited from Middle English oftentymes. By surface analysis, oftentime + -s. Compare oftentime. Compare also German oftmals, Middle French souventesfois.
oftentimes.x: Pique and linen also accented several coats and oftentimes were both detachable and formed an overcollar covering a collar made from the coat fabric.

ointment.e: A later form (as if oint + -ment) of Middle English oinement, borrowed from Old French oignement (“an anointing”), from oigner, oindre, ongier (“to anoint”), from Latin…
ointment.x: The doctor prescribed an antibiotic ointment for the wound.

oldness.e: From Middle English oldnesse, from Old English ealdnes, ealdnyss (“oldness; age”), equivalent to old + -ness.
oldness.x: This policy and reverence of age makes the world bitter to the best of our times; keeps our fortunes from us till our oldness cannot relish them.

oligarch.e: From French oligarque, olygarche, from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs). By surface analysis, olig- (“few”) + -arch (“ruler, leader”).
oligarch.x: Millions of people were starving, while the oligarchs and their supporters were surfeiting on the surplus.

oligarchy.e: Borrowed from French oligarchie, from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía), from ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).
oligarchy.x: The Itasca Project is just one example of existing oligarchy, and a surprisingly open one at that.

olive.x: Trevor, like an Aussie outbacker, eats snacks and a pickup meal of bread, cantaloupe, olives, mangoes, and melon.

olivine.x: The olivine crystals in most basalts are imperfect, lacking clear crystal faces.

omega.e: From Middle English, from Ancient Greek ὦ μέγα (ô méga), meaning “great ω” (omega is a long vowel in Ancient Greek).
omega.x: The fact that the letter was incised above the line indicates that it is probably an omega.

omelette.e: First attested in 1611; borrowed from French omelette, see which for further etymology.
omelette.x: She had never meant to confide in him — certainly not here, eating omelette and cheese sauce — but that look seemed to demand a confidence.

ominous.e: From Latin ōminōsus (“full of foreboding”), from ōmen (“forbidden fruit, omen”), from Old Latin osmen, of uncertain origin, with many origins proposed (see ōmen).

omission.e: From Middle English omissioun, from Old French omission, from Late Latin omissio, omissionem, from Latin omitto.
omission.x: Scots was not ‘banned’ outright — impossible anyway with so many Scots-speaking teachers but, like Gaelic, marginalised by omission.

omnibus.x: This work is an omnibus containing all books in the Remembrance of Earth’s Past series.

omnipotence.e: From Late Middle English omnipotens, from Old French omnipotence, from Latin omnipotentia.

omnipotent.e: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.
omnipotent.x: All the spirits of the elements bowed down before him; but the future was still hidden from his eyes, and Death was omnipotent.

omnipresent.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns, equivalent to omni- + present.
omnipresent.x: That's especially critical in a world where cruelty, war and bad news seem omnipresent.

omniscience.e: From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).
omniscience.x: Many people believe in God's omniscience.

omniscient.e: From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).
omniscient.x: The story was narrated from an omniscient point of view.

omnivore.e: From the Latin omnivorus. By surface analysis, omni- + -vore.
omnivore.x: Bears are omnivores: they can eat plants, but they also eat fish.

onanism.e: From Onan + -ism. In the Book of Genesis, Onan, son of Judah, in fulfillment of the laws of levirate marriage was to impregnate his brother Er's widow, Tamar, in order to…

oncology.e: First attested 1857. By surface analysis, onco- + -logy.

oneness.e: From Middle English oonnesse, onnesse, from Old English ānnes (“oneness, unity, agreement, covenant, solitude”), from Proto-West Germanic *ainnassī (“oneness”)…

onerous.x: Again, and more intensely than ever, she desired a fixed occupation,—no matter how onerous, how irksome.

onesie.e: Genericized trademark from the Gerber Childrenswear brand name Onesies, which became reinterpreted as a plural. Equivalent to one + -sie.

ongoing.e: From on + going, related to the phrasal verb go on.
ongoing.x: "Major refurbishments will be made over the next ten years. We have nine wooden viaducts along the line - it's an ongoing programme," he says.

onigiri.x: He cooks his breakfast of rice and misoshiru and packs onigiri rice balls for his lunch.

onion.e: From Middle English onyoun, oynoun, from Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem, accusative of ūniō (“onion”), which had also been borrowed into Old English as yne…
onion.x: Some of the weeds that cause an undesirable flavor in milk are: onion, tarweed, scaleweed, garlic, mustard, pepper grass.

onsen.e: From Japanese 温泉 (onsen), from Middle Chinese 溫泉 ('won dzjwen, “hot springs”), from 溫 /温 (wēn, “warm”) + 泉 (quán, “spring[s]”).
onsen.x: The hottest springs in Japan aren't in the north but at the Obama Onsen outside Nagasaki.

onset.e: From on- + set. Compare Old English onsettan (“to impose; oppress, bear down”).
onset.x: There is surely no greater wisdom than well to time the beginnings and onsets of things.

onslaught.e: From on- + slaught. Formed after Middle Dutch aenslag, aenslach, equivalent to aen + slag, although slaught corresponds to Middle Dutch slacht.
onslaught.x: They opened the doors and prepared for the onslaught of holiday shoppers.

ontology.x: The answer to the controversial question of whether Aristotle's ontology includes non-substantial particulars, then, is that it does.

opacity.e: From opaque + -ity, from French opacité, from Latin opācitās, from opācus.
opacity.x: The opacity of a clean glass window is near zero.

opener.e: From Middle English oppinnare, opynnare, from Old English openere, equivalent to open + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).
opener.x: The late-night openers in the mall include two restaurants and a clothing store.

openly.e: From Middle English openli, from Old English openlīċe. By surface analysis, open + -ly.
openly.x: We must speak our minds openly, debate our disagreements honestly, but always pursue solidarity.

openness.e: From Middle English *opennesse, from Old English openness (“openness, publicity”), equivalent to open + -ness.

operational.x: Despite somewhat faded paintwork, 87017 Iron Duke is clearly very much operational, as confirmed here on September 4.

opine.e: Borrowed from Middle French opiner, from Latin opīnor (“to hold as an opinion”), from *opīnus (“thinking, expecting”), only in negative nec-opīnus (“not expecting”) and…
opine.x: I opined that matters would soon become considerably worse.

opium.x: Opium is largely used by the Chinese as a sexual provocation, both by men and women.

opponent.e: Borrowed from Latin oppōnēns (“opposing”), present active participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”).
opponent.x: The person who ran against her in the last election proved to be a formidable opponent.

opportune.e: From Old French opportun, from Latin opportunus.
opportune.x: This would be an opportune spot for a picnic.

opportunism.e: From French opportunisme, equivalent to opportune + -ism.

opportunist.e: From French opportuniste, equivalent to opportune + -ist.

oppose.e: From Middle English opposen, from Old French opposer, from Latin ob (“before, against”) + Medieval Latin pono (“to put”), taking the place of Latin opponere (“to…
oppose.x: There is still time to oppose this plan.

opposition.e: From Middle English opposicioun, from Old French oposicion (whence French opposition), from Late Latin oppositiō, translating Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from…
opposition.x: The two politicians are in opposition to the bill.

oppress.e: From Middle English oppressen, from Old French oppresser, from Medieval Latin oppressare (“to press against, oppress”), frequentative of Latin opprimere, past participle…
oppress.x: The rural poor were oppressed by the land-owners.

oppressed.x: The novel tells the story of an oppressed community.

oppression.e: From Middle English oppression, from Old French oppression, from Latin oppressiō (“a pressing down, violence, oppression”), from opprimō; see oppress.
oppression.x: Extreme freedom is followed by extreme oppression, said Plato.

oppressive.x: The oppressive tax laws made it difficult to start a small company.

oppressor.e: From Middle English oppressour, from Old French opressor and Latin oppressor; equivalent to oppress + -or.
oppressor.x: All members of society are hurt by the dynamic of oppressor versus oppressed (McIntosh, 1988).

optical.x: A microscope is an optical instrument.

optics.e: From Medieval Latin opticus (“optic, optical”), from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós), equivalent to optic + -ics.
optics.x: The optics of this telescope are particularly good.

optimal.x: Finding the optimal balance between features and price is a common problem.

optimism.e: From French optimisme, equivalent to Latin optimus + -ism.
optimism.x: I love her youth, her beauty and above all her optimism that everything will turn out fine.

optimize.x: We need to optimize the supply chain to reduce costs.

optional.x: On that beach clothing is entirely optional.

opulent.e: Borrowed from Latin opulēns, opulentus, from ops (“wealth, power, resources”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃op- (“to work; produce in abundance”).

oracle.e: From Middle English oracle, from Old French oracle m, from Latin ōrāculum n.
oracle.x: The oracles are dumb; / No voice or hideous hum / Runs through the arched roof in words deceiving.

orally.x: This medicine is taken orally. Swallowing a pill sure beats getting a shot every day.

orangutan.e: Probably via Dutch orang-oetan, orang-oetang, apparently from Malay orang hutan, orang utan (literally “forest person”), from orang (“person, man”) + hutan (“forest”)…

oration.e: Borrowed from Latin ōrātiō, ōrātiōnem, from ōrō (“to orate”) + -tiō (“action (nominalizer)”). Cognate with and doublet of orison.
oration.x: And vpon a ſet day Herod arayed in royall apparell, ſate vpon his throne, and made an Oration vnto them.

orator.e: From Middle English oratour, from Anglo-Norman oratour, from Latin ōrātor.

oratorio.e: Borrowed from Italian oratorio (“oratorical”), from Latin ōrātōrius. Doublet of oratory.

oratory.e: From Middle English oratorie, from Anglo-Norman oratorie, Middle French oratoire, and their source, Late Latin ōrātōrium. Doublet of oratorio.

orbit.x: The Moon's orbit around the Earth takes nearly one month to complete.

orbital.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin orbitālis, from orbita (“a track or rut; a circuit, orbit”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to orbit + -al.
orbital.x: The M25 is an orbital motorway around London.

orchard.e: From Middle English orchard, orcherd, from Old English orċeard, ortġeard, a compound of *ort (probably from Proto-Germanic *urtiz, a dissimilated variant of…

orchestra.e: Borrowed from Latin orchēstra, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra), from ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai, “to dance”) + -τρᾰ (-tră, “a suffix used to form instrument…
orchestra.x: The orchestra plays music for the dancers to dance to in the 19th century-styled dance hall.

orchestrate.e: From orchestra + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French orchestrer.
orchestrate.x: Sergio Leone orchestrated "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly".

orchid.e: From New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”) (ostensibly from the shape of the…

ordain.e: From Middle English ordeynen, from Old French ordiner, from Latin ordinare (“to order”), from ordo (“order”). Doublet of ordinate.

ordeal.e: From Middle English ordel, ordal, from Medieval Latin ordālium or inherited from its source Old English ordēl, ordāl (“ordeal, judgement”), from Proto-West Germanic…

orderly.x: He has always kept an orderly kitchen, with nothing out of place.

ordinance.e: From Middle English ordinaunce (ca. 1300), from Old French ordenance (“decree, command”) (modern French ordonnance), from Medieval Latin ordinantia, from ordinans, the…
ordinance.x: Alderman Richard Mell then pushed through antipeddling ordinances in the 33rd and 47th wards.

ordination.e: From Middle French ordination, from Old French ordinacion, from Latin ordinatio.

ordnance.e: A reduced form of ordinance, which is attested from the late 14th century in the sense of “military equipment or provisions”.

oregano.e: 18th century, from Spanish orégano (“wild marjoram”), from Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὀρίγανον (oríganon). Doublet of origanum.

organic.e: From Middle English organic, organik, from Old French organique, from Latin organicus.
organic.x: Most types of German field divisions include an organic reconnaissance battalion, and the remainder have strong reconnaissance companies.

organism.e: First attested in 1701; from organ + -ism, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “a tool, instrument”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“work”).

organist.e: From Middle French organiste, from Medieval Latin organista. By surface analysis, organ + -ist.

organizational.x: They changed the company's organizational structure.

organize.e: From Middle English organizen, organysen, partly from Middle French organiser and partly from its etymon, Medieval Latin organizō, from Latin organum (“organ”).
organize.x: This original and supreme will organizes the government.

organizer.x: I'll add that meeting to my organizer.

orgasm.x: Never had I experienced such an immense slow orgasm – its ripples ran like the tributaries of the Nile throughout the whole nervous system.

orgasmic.e: From Ancient Greek. The historically "correct" form is orgastic.
orgasmic.x: Seemingly every year, another study announces that married women are more orgasmic than single women.

orientation.x: The homing instinct in pigeons is an example of orientation.

orienteering.e: Borrowed from Swedish orientering, from orientera (“orient, orientate”) + -ing.

orifice.e: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).
orifice.x: The plug in the orifice of the tube was temporarily removed and the mirror carefully cleaned.

origami.e: Borrowed from Japanese 折(お)り紙(がみ) (origami), from 折(お)り (ori, “to fold”) + 紙(かみ) (kami, “paper”).
origami.x: The production notes are folded like the funny origamis that I made in grammar school (only I used to write boy's names inside each section).

origin.e: From Middle English origine, origyne, from Old French origine, orine, ourine, from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, birth, origin”), from orior (“to rise”); see orient.
origin.x: The custom has its origin in ancient Greece.

originality.e: From French originalité. By surface analysis, original + -ity.
originality.x: Originality may be the capacity to look at the same facts and see new explanations.

originate.e: From Medieval Latin orīginātus, perfect passive participle of orīginō (“to begin, give rise to”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from orīgō (orīgin- in…
originate.x: Einstein originated the theory of relativity.

originator.x: Another perfume was known as nicerotiana, named after its originator Nicerotas.

oriole.e: A borrowing from Middle French oriol, from Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus, diminutive of aureus (“golden”). Doublet of aureole. First use appears c.
oriole.x: Those at risk include the wood thrush, a well-known songbird, and the Baltimore oriole, the mascot of Maryland’s baseball team.

ornament.e: From Middle English ornament, from Old French ornement, from Latin ornamentum (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from ornāre (“to…
ornament.x: I'm a bit short on brain myself; the old bean would appear to have been constructed more for ornament than for use.

ornamental.x: Some think it most ornamental to wear their bracelets on their wrists; others, about their ankles.

ornithology.e: From New Latin ornithologia, coined by Ulisse Aldrovandi from Ancient Greek ὀρνιθολόγος (ornithológos), from ὄρνις (órnis) and λόγος (lógos). See also ornitho- + -logy.

ornithopter.e: From French ornithoptère, from Ancient Greek ὄρνιθ- (órnith-) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”), equivalent to ornitho- + -pter.

orphan.e: Late Middle English, from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos.

orthodox.e: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós…

orthodoxy.e: From Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía), from ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) + δόξα (dóxa, “way, opinion”). By surface analysis, orthodox + -y.
orthodoxy.x: The two concepts are so distinct within Christianity that they have different names — orthodoxy (right belief) and orthopraxy (right conduct).

orthopedics.e: From ortho- + Ancient Greek παιδεία (paideía, “upbringing, training”). Originally a branch of medicine correcting deformities in children.

ortolan.e: From Middle French hortolan (“gardener”), from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortulan.

oscillate.e: First attested in 1726; borrowed from Latin ōscillātus, perfect passive participle of Latin ōscillō (“to swing”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ōscillum (“a…
oscillate.x: A pendulum oscillates slower as it gets longer.

oscillation.e: From French oscillation, from Latin oscillatio, from Latin oscillo. By surface analysis, oscillate + -ion.

oscillator.x: He has turned up a number of new oscillators of periods 2,3,4,5,6, & 8.

osmium.x: Their latest catalyst includes some osmium.

osmosis.e: From endosmose and exosmose, both coined by French physician Henri Dutrochet in 1826.
osmosis.x: I was reading about chickens, and I guess I learned about hawks through osmosis.

osprey.e: From Late Middle English ospray, from Anglo-Norman ospriet, from Medieval Latin avis praedae (“bird of prey”), a generic term apparently confused with this specific bird…
osprey.x: 1594, George Peele (attributed), The Battle of Alcazar I will provide thee of a princely osprey.

ossuary.e: From Late Latin ossuārium (“charnel house”), from ossuārius (“of or for bones”), from compound of Latin os (“bone”) + adjectival suffix -ārius (“of, related to”).

ostensible.e: Borrowed from French ostensible, formed with the suffix -ible, from Latin ostensus, the past participle of ostendō (“show”), itself from obs- (“in front of”) (akin to ob-…
ostensible.x: The ostensible reason for his visit to New York was to see his mother, but the real reason was to get to the Yankees game the next day.

ostentation.e: Originated 1425–75 from late Middle English ostentacioun, borrowed from Middle French ostentation and its etymon Latin ostentātiō, ostentātiōnem, equivalent to ostentātus…
ostentation.x: At times there are more than 100 deer on his property and an ostentation of peacocks.

osteoporosis.e: From Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”) + Ancient Greek πώρωσις (pṓrōsis, “petrification, callousness”), from Ancient Greek πῶρος (pôros, “tuff, a porous type of…

osteosarcoma.x: Even small osteosarcomas can be unimaginably painful.

ostracism.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀστρακισμός (ostrakismós, “banishment by means of voting with pot shards”), from ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “ostracize”) + -ισμός (-ismós…

ostrich.e: From Middle English ostrich, ostriche, ostryche, ostrige, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ostrige and Old French ostruce, from Vulgar Latin *austruthio, from Latin avis…

otherworldly.e: From other world (“a world beyond death; a world other than the everyday world”) + -ly (suffix meaning having the likeness of, resembling forming adjectives).

ottoman.e: From Ottoman in the early 19th century; so named because reclining on a couch was associated with Middle Eastern customs.
ottoman.x: A 39-year-old British woman was killed when a malfunctioning ottoman bed fell on her neck and asphyxiated her, a coroner’s report said.

ounce.e: From Middle English ounce, unce, from Middle French once, from Latin ū̆ncia (“Roman ounce, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”).
ounce.x: He didn't feel even an ounce of regret for his actions.

outburst.e: Inherited from Middle English outbersten, outbresten. Cognate with Dutch uitbarsten (“to erupt; burst out”), German ausbersten (“to burst out; erupt”).

outcast.e: From Middle English outcasten, equivalent to out- + cast.
outcast.x: It means equal ruin to me, as the world reckons it — outcasting, the loss of my appointment, the breaking off my life's work. I pay my price.

outcome.x: A quality automobile is the outcome of the work of skilled engineers and thousands of workers.

outdated.x: His outdated wordprocessing software could not read the files I sent.

outdoors.e: From out + doors (plural of door), probably as a shortening of out of doors. Alternatively, from outdoor (adjective) + -s (adverbial genitive suffix).
outdoors.x: They went outdoors to light up their cigarettes.

outgoing.x: Tom is very outgoing and enjoys meeting people; his brother, on the other hand, is painfully shy.

outhouse.e: From Middle English outhous, equivalent to out- + house. Compare Old Norse úthús (“outhouse”).

outing.e: From out + -ing. Compare Old English yting ("outing, journey").
outing.x: This was a fine day's outing for anybody who had been cooped up in the shops for a few months.

outlaw.e: From Middle English outlawe, outlagh, utlaȝe, from Old English ūtlaga (“outlaw”), borrowed from Old Norse útlagi (“outlaw, fugitive”), equivalent to out- + law.
outlaw.x: The main character in the play was a bit of an outlaw who refused to shake hands or say thank you.

outlay.x: Without too much outlay, you could buy a second-hand car.

outlet.e: From Middle English outlete, outeleate, ut-lete, derived from Middle English outleten (“to allow, let out, emit”), equivalent to out- + let.
outlet.x: Jamie found doing martial arts was a great outlet for her stress.

outline.x: From this point of vantage, we were able to gain an impression of the massive outlines of the main structure, and its intricate maze of girders.

outlive.e: From Middle English outliven, equivalent to out- + live.
outlive.x: And he that calls on thee, let him bring forth / Eternal numbers to outlive long date.

outpost.x: The outpost did not have enough ammunition to resist a determined assault.

output.e: From out + (verb) put; nominalisation of put out.
output.x: The factory increased its output this year.

outrageous.e: From Anglo-Norman outrageus, Middle French outrageus, from outrage; equivalent to outrage + -ous.
outrageous.x: "It's something I really am quite nervous about," he admits, before adding, with relish: "You have to be a bit outrageous and challenging sometimes."

outrigger.e: Modification of earlier outligger after rig (“to fit out”); equivalent to out- + ligger.
outrigger.x: The cranes are supplied with outriggers and jacks for use when lifting heavy loads or when working at extended radii.

outright.e: From Middle English outright. By surface analysis, out + right.

outsider.x: While the initiated easily understand the symbols, they are wholly inaccessible to outsiders.

outskirts.x: He lived on the outskirts of Paris for a time.

outsource.x: They decided to outsource the design and manufacture of the system to a vendor.

outspoken.e: From outspeak, equivalent to out- + spoken.
outspoken.x: Critics were vehemently outspoken; but while they fretted about looks, they missed the cleverer points in the design itself.

outstanding.e: From outstand, equivalent to out- + standing or outstand + -ing.
outstanding.x: I have several outstanding tasks on my to-do list.

outward.e: From Middle English outward, from Old English ūtweard, equivalent to out + -ward.
outward.x: The wrong side may be turned outward.

ovary.e: From New Latin ovarium, from Medieval Latin ovaria (“bird ovary”), from Latin ovum (“egg”). Doublet of ovarium.

ovation.e: From Late Latin ovatio (“egg-laying”) + English -ion (suffix indicating an action or process, or the result of an action or process).

overall.e: From Middle English overall, overal, from Old English ofer eall, ofer ealle (“over all”), equivalent to over + all.
overall.x: "The cranium is clearly plesiomorphic in overall form, presenting primitive traits shared by earlier hominins," the authors wrote.

overcharge.e: From Middle English overchargen, equivalent to over- + charge.
overcharge.x: "It's about decades of an office that overcharges and oversentences but keeps getting worse results," Conklin says.

overdo.e: From Middle English overdon, from Old English oferdōn, equivalent to over- + do.
overdo.x: And you’re so weak I’le not pursue you, For fear lest I should overdo you.

overdraft.x: The bank have given me an overdraft of $2000.

overestimate.x: I overestimated the number of attendees, and bought far too much food for the party.

overflow.e: From Middle English overflowen, from Old English oferflōwan, equivalent to over- + flow.

overhead.e: From Middle English owerheved, over-hed, over hede (adverb), from Old English oferhēafod (adverb), equivalent to over- + head.
overhead.x: Place your luggage in the overhead lockers.

overhear.e: From Middle English overheren, from Old English oferhīeran (“to overhear, hear, disobey, disregard, neglect”), equivalent to over- + hear.
overhear.x: I was hanging clothes in the garden and I overheard the neighbours talking about Sheila's pregnancy.

overheat.e: From Middle English overheten. Cognate with German überheizen, überhitzen (“to overheat”), Swedish överhetta (“to overheat”). By surface analysis, over- + heat.
overheat.x: 'Made one quite thankful to get back to the fug, though as a rule I think the way these trains are overheated is something scandalous'.

overlap.e: From over- + lap. Cognate with Dutch overlap.

overlord.e: From Middle English oferrlaferrd, orlard, our-lord, ouyr-lord, equivalent to over- + lord.
overlord.x: The various tribal chieftains met each spring to elect an overlord that would lead them in time of war.

overly.x: Parents can be overly protective of their children.

overpass.x: The homeless man had built a little shelter, complete with cook-stove, beneath a concrete overpass.

overpower.x: We overpowered the opposing army within a couple of hours.

overrated.x: I say, “Tom Cruise,” because I know Irene hates Tom Cruise and she'll go on and on about why he's completely overrated.

overreact.x: Please try not to overreact if she drives badly when she is first learning.

override.e: From Middle English overriden, from Old English oferrīdan, equivalent to over- + ride. Cognate with Dutch overrijden, German überreiten, Danish override.
override.x: In automotive design, safety should override lesser factors such as cosmetics and corner-cutting.

overseas.e: From earlier oversea, equivalent to oversea + -s. Compare West Frisian oerseesk, Dutch overzees, German Übersee, Danish oversøisk.
overseas.x: Overseas branches of the company are doing well.

oversee.e: From Middle English overseen, ouverseen, from Old English ofersēon (“to observe, oversee; to overlook, neglect”), equivalent to over- + see.
oversee.x: It is congress's duty to oversee the spending of federal funds.

overshadow.e: From Middle English overschadwen, overschadewe, from Old English ofersċeadwian (“to overshadow”), equivalent to over- + shadow.

oversight.e: From over- + sight. Verb sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Aufsicht.
oversight.x: A small oversight at this stage can lead to big problems later.

overstep.e: From Middle English *oversteppen, from Old English ofersteppan, from Proto-Germanic *uberstapjaną (“to step over; overstep”).
overstep.x: That color scheme really oversteps the bounds of good taste.

overt.e: From Middle English overt, uverte (“open, uncovered; unfastened; accessible, unobstructed.
overt.x: Arg. an eagle rising wings overt inverted sa. armed or. HILTOFTE, V.

overtake.e: From Middle English overtaken, likely a replacement alteration (as the Middle English verb taken replaced nimen (“to take”)), of Middle English overnimen (“to overtake”)…

overthrow.e: From Middle English overthrowen, equivalent to over- + throw. Compare Dutch overdraaien, German überdrehen, Old English oferweorpan (“to overthrow”).
overthrow.x: I hate the current government, but not enough to want to overthrow them.

overtime.x: Workers are usually paid extra for working overtime.

overtone.e: From over- + tone, calque of German Oberton.

overture.e: From Middle English overture, from Anglo-Norman, Middle French overture, from Old French overture, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture.
overture.x: My mother had no choice; one did not turn down such an overture from the regent.

overweight.x: Before her diet, Jane was noticeably overweight, but she shed five kilos in the next two months.

overwhelming.x: The vote was taken at once, and it was agreed by an overwhelming majority that rats were comrades.

ownership.x: The successful candidate will take ownership of all internal design projects.

oxidation.e: From French oxydation, equivalent to oxide + -ation. See oxidate.

oxide.x: Most metals, when subjected to heat until they become melted, combine with oxygen of the atmosphere, and form what are called oxides.

oximeter.e: From oxi- (variant of oxy-) + -meter. The word was first applied in sense 2 (“a device that measures the oxygen saturation of arterial blood”) by American physiologist…
oximeter.x: At 8 to 10 G, ear oximeter readings may fall to 75 percent saturation. The lungs, afterward, may show some atelectasis.

oxtail.e: From Middle English ox tayll, from Old English oxan tæġl (literally “ox's tail”), equivalent to ox + tail.

oxymoron.e: First attested in the 17th century, noun use of 5th century Latin oxymōrum (adjective), neut. nom.
oxymoron.x: In Oxymoron jarring phrases join And terms opposed in harmony combine.

oxytocin.e: From oxytocic, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “swift”) + τόκος (tókos, “childbirth”, from τίκτω (tíktō, “I give birth”)).

oyster.x: He was a bold man that first ate an oyster.

ozone.e: From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent…
ozone.x: Lightning flashed again, the thunder came a second later. It rained harder. The smell of ozone was strong. You could feel the charge in the air.
